title: Use mathematics to investigate and monitor the financial aspects of personal, business, national and international issues

lessons.title: Interest, inflation and the time value of money
lessons.html:
Money changes value over time

A rand today is worth more than a rand next year, because money can earn interest and because prices rise. Farm supervisors and managers deal with this every day: production loans, hire-purchase on a tractor, savings for the next season and rising input prices.

Simple interest

Interest is calculated only on the original amount (the principal).

I = P × i × n, where P = principal, i = interest rate per year as a decimal, n = number of years.

Example: R50 000 invested at 10% simple interest for 3 years: I = 50 000 × 0.10 × 3 = R15 000. The total is R65 000.

Compound interest

Interest is added to the balance, and next period's interest is calculated on the new balance.

A = P × (1 + i) to the power n, where A is the final amount. In other words, multiply P by (1 + i) once for every year.

Example: R50 000 at 10% compounded yearly for 3 years: A = 50 000 × 1.10 × 1.10 × 1.10 = R66 550. Compounding earned R1 550 more than simple interest. On loans the same effect works against you: unpaid interest grows quickly, which is why an overdue production account becomes expensive.

If interest is compounded monthly, divide the yearly rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12.

Inflation

Inflation is the general rise in prices, measured in South Africa by Stats SA as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It is calculated in the same way as compound growth. If diesel costs R22.00 a litre and rises by 6% in a year, next year's price is 22.00 × 1.06 = R23.32. If your wage increase is lower than inflation, your real income falls, even though the rand amount goes up.

Percentage change

Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. If the maize price moves from R3 800 to R4 180 per ton, the change is 380 ÷ 3 800 × 100 = 10%.

Depreciation

Machinery loses value. With straight-line depreciation the same amount is written off each year: a tractor bought for R900 000 with an expected value of R180 000 after 8 years loses (900 000 − 180 000) ÷ 8 = R90 000 per year. With reducing-balance depreciation at 20%, its value after one year is R720 000 and after two years R576 000.

lessons.title: Budgets, costs and break-even on the farm
lessons.html:
Planning money for a person and a business

Personal budget

A budget lists expected income and expenses for a period. Start with net pay (after PAYE, UIF and other deductions), then list fixed expenses (rent, transport, school fees, funeral policy) and variable expenses (food, electricity, airtime). If expenses are higher than income, you are borrowing, often on expensive store or micro-lender credit. Compare the interest rate and total cost of credit, not only the monthly instalment.

Enterprise budget

A farm enterprise budget shows income and costs per hectare or per animal.

Item (per ha, maize)Amount (R)
Income: 6 t × R3 90023 400
Seed, fertiliser, chemicals11 500
Fuel, repairs, contractors4 200
Total directly allocable costs15 700
Gross margin7 700

The gross margin must still pay overheads such as permanent salaries, insurance and interest. The figures above are an example only; use your own farm's records and current prices.

Fixed and variable costs

Variable costs change with output (feed, seed, packaging). Fixed costs stay the same whatever you produce (rent, insurance, depreciation).

Break-even

Break-even quantity = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit). Example: a small feedlot has fixed costs of R240 000 a year and makes R4 000 per ton of product with variable costs of R2 500 per ton. Break-even = 240 000 ÷ 1 500 = 160 tons. Below 160 tons it loses money; above it, it makes a profit.

Cash flow

Farms can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash, because costs are paid at planting and income comes at harvest. A monthly cash-flow budget shows when an overdraft or production loan is needed and how much interest it will cost. Monitor actual figures against budget each month and explain large differences (variances).

Using graphs

Plot monthly income and expenses on a line graph, or costs per hectare on a bar graph. Graphs make trends visible quickly, but always check the scale on the axes before you draw conclusions.

lessons.title: Tax, exchange rates and the wider economy
lessons.html:
National and international money matters

VAT

Value-Added Tax in South Africa is currently 15% on most goods and services. Some basic foods are zero-rated. To add VAT: price including VAT = price excluding VAT × 1.15, so R1 000 becomes R1 150. To find the VAT inside a VAT-inclusive price, multiply by 15 and divide by 115: R1 150 × 15 ÷ 115 = R150. VAT-registered farms claim back VAT paid on inputs, so keep valid tax invoices.

Income tax

Personal income tax uses tax brackets: higher portions of income are taxed at higher rates, and rebates reduce the tax payable. SARS publishes the tables every year after the Budget speech. Always use the current year's table; do not reuse old rates.

Exchange rates

Many farm inputs (fuel, fertiliser, chemicals, machinery) are priced from imports in US dollars, and many products (citrus, wine, wool, macadamias) are exported. An exchange rate tells you how many rand buy one unit of foreign currency.

  • An export carton of citrus sold for $12 at R18.50 per dollar earns 12 × 18.50 = R222.
  • If the rand strengthens to R17.00 per dollar, the same carton earns R204, which is R18 less.
  • A weaker rand helps exporters but makes imported inputs more expensive.

To convert rand to dollars, divide: R37 000 ÷ 18.50 = $2 000.

National indicators

  • Gross Domestic Product (GDP) – the total value of goods and services produced in the country. Agriculture's share is small but it is important for jobs, exports and food security.
  • Inflation (CPI) – affects wage negotiations and input costs.
  • The repo rate – set by the South African Reserve Bank; banks' prime lending rate moves with it, which changes the cost of farm loans.

Reading financial news critically

When you see a claim such as ‘food prices up 12%’, ask: compared with when? Which products? Is it a nominal or real change? Is the graph's axis starting at zero? Good financial mathematics means checking the numbers before acting on them.

Key points

  • Simple interest: I = P × i × n; compound growth: A = P × (1 + i) to the power n.
  • Inflation and depreciation are calculated with the same percentage methods.
  • Break-even = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit).
  • VAT at 15%: multiply by 1.15 to add it; multiply by 15/115 to find it in an inclusive price.
  • A weaker rand raises export income and the cost of imported inputs.
